newsitem.title: MACAU: After Hong Kong rejoins China, Macau is next.
newsitem.headline: After Hong Kong rejoins China, Macau is next.

text.p: "I think it is a precious gift that China has given us," freelance political commentator Johnny Un says about Macau, which reverts to China two and a half years after Hong Kong.

"Macau will be able to learn from Hong Kong's experience under Chinese rule for over two years before its own reversion," says Un, who has worked previously as a reporter in Hong Kong, Macau and the United States.
Under the Sino-Portuguese Joint Declaration of 1987, Macau will revert to China at midnight December 19, 1999, long after Hong Kong returns to China on July 1.

Unlike Hong Kong, Macau's handover will not be a transfer of sovereignty but merely a change in administration since the region of 455,000 residents is no longer a Portuguese colony but a Chinese territory under Portuguese administration.

Lisbon relinquished sovereignty over Macau after its anti-colonialist 1974 Revolution of the Carnations, but Beijing has pledged not to exercise sovereignty until the transfer of administration in 1999.
The year 1999 was chosen because China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping wanted China reunified before the turn of the century, according to Portuguese sources.
Both sides also settled on December 19 because it would allow the outgoing Portuguese administration to return home before Christmas that year.
The history of how Hong Kong and Macau came under foreign rule is also starkly different.
While Britain wrested Hong Kong from China as war booty after the infamous 19th century Opium Wars, the Macau peninsula was peacefully settled by Portuguese seafarers around 1557.

Macau's two off-shore islands, Taipa and Coloane, came under Portuguese administration in 1847 and 1864 respectively, after their inhabitants asked the Portuguese garrison on the peninsula for protection against Chinese pirates.

"Macau and Hong Kong have different histories. Unlike between Britain and China, there was never a military conflict between Portugal and China," said former Macau mayor Joaquim Morais Alves, 74, now an appointed deputy to the Macau assembly.
"The Opium Wars were deplorable," Alves said, stressing that Sino-Portuguese relations over Macau "have always been based on amicable dialogue and mutual understanding."

China's revolutionary leader Mao Zedong said in the past Portugal was the only Western colonial power that never waged war on China. Macau is Europe's oldest existing outpost in Asia. When Britain seized Hong Kong in 1841, Portuguese rule had already been in place in Macau for 284 years.
The enclave's residents - Chinese, Portuguese and Eurasians - say China allowed Portuguese rule to stay for over four centuries because both sides had always been on friendly terms.
There were of course the odd quarrels, like the time in 1849 when two Chinese bounty hunters beheaded a Macau governor when he failed to consult Chinese mandarins on major policy changes.

Macau's Portuguese-administration has customarily sought China's consent on all major policy decisions and projects before implementing them, especially since the signing of the Sino-Portuguese Joint Declaration in 1987, which detailed Macau's eventual return to China.
About one-third of the legislature has been directly elected by universal suffrage since 1976, almost two decades before Britain allowed direct elections in 1995 in Hong Kong.
Macau residents also observe Hong Kong's Western-style confrontational party politics and anti-China rallies with a mixture of bewilderment, awe and condemnation.

Anti-Chinese protests are almost non-existent in Macau. Even the tiny pro-democracy movement considers itself to be as patriotic as Beijing's ubiquitous united front neighbourhood, business and labour associations in the enclave.

Macau's community leaders have even set up a special committee to celebrate Hong Kong's return to China. Among its members are casino mogul Stanley Ho, Catholic Bishop Domingos Lam and banking association chairman Edmund Ho Hau Wah, who is widely tipped to become Macau's first post-handover leader.

"Unlike Hong Kong, most Macau Chinese have patriotic feelings about their motherland because most Chinese schools in Macau always followed the mainland's history," said U Tak Hon, chief reporter with the Va Kio Pou daily.
Observers say virtually all Macau Chinese accept the territory's return to China as a necessity. But Macau's non-Chinese minorities are anxious.
Alves said he had the "right to feel sad" about Macau's return to China as "nothing is certain" about Macau's future.
Some community leaders said Macau could learn from Hong Kong's experience in public administration and social welfare.
"The British were very bad when they killed thousands of Chinese in the Opium Wars but later they did many great things in Hong Kong," said Portuguese civil servant Joaquim Simoes.
